head: afe50cffca6b52fbcc79326b85f8c0ad0e5a40cf
note: Amended c8 after pass 5 graded it unmet and was right to. It read 'No recorded fact and no refusal is derived from git ... git is referenced as evidence by sha'; c11 requires every event to name its branch, which resolveConfig defaults from git.branch(). A branch name is not a sha, so no implementation could satisfy both clauses. Measured before amending: exactly four values reach storage from git - event.head, closedCommit, and an audit pass's base/head are all shas and were always permitted; event.branch was the only one that was not, and it is provenance rather than a claim about the work. c8 now prohibits refusals and facts about the work, and permits an inferred default argument that records where a write happened. The substance is untouched and was independently verified by the same pass: every git-derived refusal about the work is gone, and every judgement in the store is one an agent made on purpose.

Measured: 15 commits this session, none touching src/scripts/content, each restating reasoning already in the spec's ## Decisions and in tasks decision. Weakening the contract would not make the store easier to write to, which is the actual diagnosis behind commit messages winning over tasks decision

note: positionalArity reads any <a|b> slot as literal subcommand keywords and counts it as zero positionals, so a usage written <id|spec> makes the command refuse its own argument. Spelled <id-or-spec> instead. Loud, not silent — the CLI answers 'unexpected argument' — so it is a naming convention to know, not a defect filed.

note: English is the only officially supported language for now. humanize cannot be made correct for other Latin-alphabet languages: its capitalisation is locale-independent (Turkish i/İ, Dutch IJ), its every-word title case is an English convention where French/Spanish/Italian/Portuguese use sentence case, and ids are ASCII-only ([a-z][a-z0-9-]*) so a word with diacritics cannot appear in one at all. Declaring another language stays accepted and falls back to keys; supporting English officially means English is what ships and what the suite proves, not that other languages are rejected.

head: 57eda4cd29f04c2c19ca6071a831efec94d2b104
note: Test drift and isolation, decided 2026-08-06 after measuring. Numbers: 28.9s wall, 175.5s summed across 69 files (~6x parallelism), transform 18.8s + import 31.6s of isolation duplication that never touches the wall, slowest file scripts/tasks/audit.test.ts at 27.2s. (1) The drift check goes in merge-ready, not audit-prompt: merge-ready already runs npm test so the numbers are free, it is the moment someone can act, and test drift is a repo property rather than a branch one. It reports the wall and the slowest file, and warns above 45s without failing the leg. The useful metric is the slowest file's absolute duration, not its share of the sum -- the wall can never drop below its slowest file, and audit.test.ts at 27.2s of a 28.9s wall is 94%, the same ratio scripts/tasks.test.ts hit at 84s of 89s before audit-loop-costs-less split it. The shape has already recurred; only the magnitude has not. (2) Isolation stays on. Turning it off attacks the 50.3s of transform+import, none of which is on the critical path -- the wall is set by one file's subprocess-spawning tests -- against real hazards: console patching, process.exitCode, cwd, and a warn-once flag needing a fresh module registry per file. Real risk, negligible reward, 90% budget headroom. (3) No test optimisation pass now. Deciding which tests are bogus or slow belongs to pre-release-readiness-audit, whose record already names reviewing whether tests protect behaviour rather than implementation and combining redundant tests without losing detection power. head: e4fc72c460ccc45c42f01a735c5fcabd32787847
note: The orchestrated run is about endurance, not cost, restated by the author 2026-08-06. Cost is already settled by docs/dsl-rewrite/delegation-experiments.md and is not what the run measures. The constraint is the human: 17 specced tasks plus ~30 miscellaneous findings, where supervising one worker costs half a day of which nearly all is reading output and saying continue, while a planning session produces a dozen specs in that same day. The human's hours are worth several times more spent planning than reviewing, so a design question settled mid-branch is paid at the expensive rate AND without the survey, prior art and rulings a planning session has in front of it. That is the double work the task system exists to prevent. Consequence: the orchestrator is a buffer, not a decision-maker - it absorbs everything that is not a genuine design decision and batches the rest into one end-of-run review. Consequence: the run's measurement is how many times a human had to enter the loop and whether planning could have prevented each, not wall-clock or audit counts.

head: e4fc72c460ccc45c42f01a735c5fcabd32787847
note: The run's corpus is the three prerequisites themselves - every-triage-action-has-a-non-interactive-form, a-clause-can-be-deferred-and-a-spec-can-carry-its-goal, a-branch-knows-which-spec-it-owes - so run-an-orchestrator-over-three-parallel-tasks requires only the-task-store-survives-parallel-branches. The old requires list named all five, which is circular once three of them are what the run works on. Their grants are disjoint after correction (triage.ts+records.ts, specDoc.ts+audit.ts, mergeReady.ts+context.ts), each landing removes friction the next round would have paid, and the isolation is real: every worktree is its own checkout, so a worker changing the task system cannot reach the orchestrator's tooling or another worker's mid-run. The run therefore proceeds WITHOUT non-interactive triage, absorbed by hand because three tasks is a batch a human can read; that capability lands from the run and is what makes the 17+30 push possible after it. clear-the-friction is dissolved rather than required.

note: Second spec defect of the round, and the audit earned its cost by finding it. c5 claimed two branches inserting adjacent ids is the ONLY remaining conflict shape. False, and I confirmed it independently: A edits r-10 while B inserts a record sorting immediately after it, swept over separations 0 to 6 -- gap 0 CONFLICTS, gap 1 and beyond merge clean. So the real condition is adjacency of changed LINES, not two inserts, and it covers three shapes: insert beside insert, edit beside insert, delete beside insert. Only the first resolves by keeping both; the other two need the edit reconciled, which c5's stated resolution does not cover. My own original measurement missed this because it only ever tested an edit FAR from an insert (records 5 and 300) and adjacency only with two inserts. Practical exposure is lower than the finding implies but real: spec-prefixed ids segregate concurrent branches into different neighbourhoods, which is why the clustering visible at docs/tasks.jsonl:559-563 -- a task record immediately above its own audit's four records -- is intra-branch and harmless. Records with generic titles carry no prefix and can collide across branches. Class: spec defect, level 1, obvious remedy, caught by audit before merge.

note: The friction channel is one system with two axes, not a class list. Does it STOP WORK (blocking / not) and WHAT IS AT FAULT (the tooling / the contract / nobody). The axes are orthogonal and each answers a different planner question: fault=tool feeds 'what do we fix', fault=contract feeds 'how do we plan differently', and blocking is purely mechanical - it decides whether dispatch halts, which isBlocked already implements. The flat four-class list this replaces (spec defect, design question, tool friction, silent guess) collapsed two independent questions into one enumeration, which is the same enumerate-instead-of-state-the-invariant mistake that produced both of this round's spec defects. RULE that falls out of the fault axis and must not be lost: a record whose fault is 'nobody, the knowledge did not exist' is NOT a defect and must not be counted as one. The author's own framing is that a spec turning out incomplete is rare, normal, and a single decision - counting those as failures would create pressure to write specs that pretend to know what they cannot, which is the opposite of what the whole round is for.

head: 01c7b4752b37ee556cce63d9b1955250e166afaa
note: Process data: the mutation-gap fix took the worker three attempts, each checked against a mutation manifest rather than assumed correct, and the two failures are worth keeping. (1) .reverse() survived - reversing only flips direction, and adjacency, which is what these tests measure, comes out right by accident. (2) A fixed-seed shuffle keyed on array LENGTH survived - two equal-length arrays always shuffle identically under a length-only seed, and both branches' arrays are equal length here, so the two inserted records still landed adjacent whether or not the sort ran. (3) A shuffle seeded from the array's own ids works, because two calls only scramble identically when given the same records. Both failures are the same species: a fixture that appears to randomise while preserving the exact property under test. Neither would have been caught by reading the test, and both were caught by mutation. This is the strongest evidence so far for keeping mutation testing in the audit loop rather than treating a green suite as proof. Class: not a defect - fault is nobody, this is the tooling working.

note: Third live instance of the spec-ownership bug, in a shape a-branch-knows-which-spec-it-owes as specced would NOT have fixed. This planning branch recorded process notes with --spec run-an-orchestrator-over-three-parallel-tasks. specsWrittenFromBranch builds its candidate list from store EVENTS carrying a spec field, so merely annotating a spec makes the branch a candidate for owing it; the file is on main so authoredAsPlan says 'not a plan'; and the spec has an open member because the orchestrated run has not happened yet. Result: the gate demands an audit of a spec whose work is deliberately scheduled for later. Clause identity as c1 specifies it does not help - this branch did not change those clauses, so c1 would also conclude 'owes'. The missing distinction is a third state. A branch can have authored a spec, or owe it, or merely have touched it, and the gate today has only the first two. The discriminator that actually works is whether THIS BRANCH'S DIFF did work against the spec's write regions - annotation leaves no code behind. Added to that spec as c7 before dispatch.

head: 5c0297614f972c9a7a72243418f08c7c48ef87a9
note: FIRST SILENT GUESS OF THE RUN, and it was found only because the audit brief asked for it explicitly. Auditing every-triage-action-has-a-non-interactive-form, the auditor answered the extra question with a genuine yes: the worker decided, by omission, that ask and redirect need no closed-record guard where defer and promote have one. Never recorded - not in the spec's Decisions, not as a decision event, not in the commit message, which explicitly notes defer's guard mirrors promote's and says nothing about leaving the other two unguarded. Reproduced: decline a record, then ask a question against it, and it exits 0, appends the question and files a triage event while the record stays declined. The printed message is honest - 'it stays declined until the question is answered' - but c4's promise is that the record stays unreviewed SO THE QUEUE KEEPS OFFERING IT, and a declined record is in no queue. The question lands where nobody will read it, which is precisely the failure every-triage-action exists to prevent. RULING: ask and redirect refuse a closed record, matching defer and promote, with the error naming the remedy. This is a design question and therefore mine, not the worker's. Validates run-an-orchestrator c5: a silent guess looks exactly like no questions, and the only reason this surfaced is that the brief went looking.

head: 07dabda6661904f989725851a5c618394f13de1d
note: Both audit findings on the clause-deferral branch and the triage branch turned on the same thing: a guard that reads as present but is reachable around. Triage's ask applied to any state, so a question could be filed against a closed record the queue would never re-offer. Clause deferral's reason requirement checks !evidence, and clauseScoped stores the raw slice untrimmed, so a whitespace-only reason passes. Neither is a coding slip - both are a check placed where the value is READ rather than where it is ASSEMBLED, which is the repository's own recorded wisdom and the thing both specs failed to state. Worth carrying into the friction channel's fault axis: these classify as contract, not worker, because in both cases the clause described the guard's effect and not the point it must act at. Verified the triage fix myself: ask on a declined record now exits 1 with a message naming the remedy, ask on an unreviewed record still exits 0, and the golden menu string is a literal rather than derived from the table under test.

head: 0ab7339b4e204a2878faeecac055b407f7f1c4ab
note: Overruled an auditor's severity judgement on a-branch-knows-which-spec-it-owes, and the reasoning is the record worth keeping. Pass 1 filed two HIGH findings and judged neither a merge blocker, on the grounds that the branch demonstrably fixes the bug it targets and both new gaps need a narrower trigger. That is sound about impact and wrong about what this branch is FOR. Its whole purpose is to make the merge gate trustworthy, and both findings are silent EXEMPTIONS - the gate waving through work it should hold - one of them inside the function this branch introduced. Trading 'wrong about half the time, loudly' for 'right nearly always, silently wrong sometimes' is not the trade the spec asked for, because a gate nobody can trust to be strict is not a gate. Both fixed before merge. Generalisable rule for the friction channel: an auditor grades a finding's blast radius well and is not positioned to weigh it against the spec's purpose, because the goal is exactly what the brief does not carry until clause deferral lands and gives it one. This is the first concrete evidence that a-clause-can-be-deferred-and-a-spec-can-carry-its-goal's second half earns its place - the auditor needed the goal to make this call and did not have it.

note: c2 of clause deferral failed a third time on control characters, and pass 3 finally produced the boundary rather than another exotic case, because the brief asked for a line with reasoning instead of confirmation of the last fix. Adopted verbatim: a reason must contain at least one character that occupies space when rendered and does not command the renderer - whitespace occupies nothing, Cf renders nothing, Cc commands rather than renders, everything else is legitimate however ugly. Also worth surfacing beyond this clause: an ESC in an evidence value lands verbatim in the spec markdown, so a reason field can paint arbitrary text in any terminal that later renders the file. That is a different class from an unreadable reason and the only one of the three narrowings that was more than tidiness.

head: 237ec4231c6d69e176b8aabc15787bb7ad956c49
note: Worker 2 caught a hazard mid-edit worth recording as a positive: its first draft of the control-character test embedded the actual raw bytes, which would have put a live ESC sequence into a tracked repo file and tripped merge-ready's own byte gate on the NUL. It noticed before committing, rewrote them as escape-sequence text, and verified byte-by-byte that none remain. Confirmed independently - zero raw control bytes in audit.test.ts, and the guard now refuses NUL BEL ESC DEL while accepting punctuation and a lone combining mark. The general shape is worth carrying: a test for a defect about dangerous input is itself a place that dangerous input gets written down, and the test file is tracked. Nothing in any brief warned about that; the worker found it by thinking about what it was typing.

head: ec2fb804fab00cc38f60581bb03cd7e3a05eb4a5
note: First narrowing of the run that fixed the RULE rather than the instance, and the method that produced it is the transferable part. c2's guard used \p{Cf} as a proxy for 'renders nothing'; Unicode defines Default_Ignorable_Code_Point which means exactly that, and 37 codepoints are default-ignorable while categorised Mn or Lo - including VS16, the ordinary emoji-presentation selector. Verified: Cf catches none of VS16, CGJ, Hangul filler, Khmer inherent vowel or Mongolian FVS; the property catches all five; emoji, CJK and Devanagari stay visible, so it is not over-broad. The three earlier narrowings each swapped one hand-picked list for a longer hand-picked list, which is why none of them held. This one swaps a category for the property that defines the concept, so a future invisible codepoint needs no edit. It happened because the brief asked the auditor to challenge the SENTENCE and set the bar explicitly - a fourth narrowing must show the rule is wrong, not that another codepoint exists. Ask for the next instance and you get one; ask whether the rule is right and you can get the rule fixed.

head: d63d440cf6def9ca989dd256b2f544b27687125d
note: Lesson-breach tracking folds into the friction channel rather than becoming a second system, and the framing matters more than the mechanism. The count is a DIAGNOSTIC FOR THE LESSON, not a scorecard for the system: 'which lesson is not landing' is actionable where 'how many defects' is not, because a lesson breached repeatedly is badly worded, in the wrong brief, or wrong, and each is fixable by editing one line. The link is cheap because the information already exists - an auditor finding a test that cannot fail IS a breach of a worker lesson, a fix-the-neighbour instance IS a breach of an auditor lesson - and only the pointer from finding to lesson is missing. Two hazards recorded so the implementer does not have to rediscover them. Zero breaches is AMBIGUOUS between the lesson working and nobody looking, so a checked-and-clean marker is required for zero to be readable; the audit brief already makes that distinction by telling auditors none-found is real only if they looked, and three audits answered the silent-guess question that way before a fourth found a real defect. And it must never gate: counting breaches while penalising them creates pressure not to report them, which costs the only honest signal there is.

head: 52bd157676085e524113e8a210b8f5724707d011
note: c7 RULING, by the author, 2026-08-06: YES, push the remaining backlog through orchestrated runs, in BATCHES OF THREE, GATED ON THE FRICTION CHANNEL LANDING FIRST. This is the decision c7 asks for and the run's terminal output. Basis: three tasks, three worktrees, 13:23-16:57 local, zero author interruptions before the batch review, against a stated baseline of half a day to supervise one worker - roughly a 4x improvement on the author's own accounting, and the only number in the run that answers the endurance question it was asked. What has to change first, and why the gate is the friction channel rather than anything else: the batch size of three was chosen in the spec for the author's hand-review capacity, but the constraint the run actually hit is different and was never recorded - THE ORCHESTRATOR'S OWN CONTEXT FILLED AT THREE TASKS PLUS ONE FOLLOW-ON. Endurance was moved off the author, which is what the branch wanted, and onto the orchestrator, which is now the binding resource. That makes the batch boundary a handoff, and today a fresh orchestrator inherits nothing queryable: 866 lines of prose in .planning/agent-feedback/tool-friction.md that no command reads. The proof that prose does not aggregate is in that file - the largest single repeated cost of the whole run, a mutation manifest that never auto-generates because 'proof: vitest <file>' names a file rather than a test, appears in eight separate pass entries at about ten minutes each and has NO open record, while a friction hit exactly once (audit-prompt's wrong WARNING) is filed high and will be fixed. So the-workflow-records-what-cost-it-in-one-place-with-one-quer is not merely the next task, it is the thing that makes orchestrator number two cheaper than number one, and the gate is set there. Second condition, from c3: the run's orchestrator adjudicated because there was no cheap route not to - a worker was blocked on a design question at 17:57Z and the only alternative to ruling was stalling it until a planning session nobody had scheduled. c3 is therefore not a discipline failure to exhort away but a missing mechanism, and its remedy is the friction channel's own blocking axis plus the unused 'question' kind. Do not dispatch a second run until a blocking question has a route that is neither 'decide it' nor 'stall the worker'.

Deferred means the branch dropped the clause and the goal survived; c3 means the orchestrator adjudicated design questions mid-branch, and c4's zero-interruption headline is only trustworthy if c3 held, so deferring c3 to buy a green gate would launder the one measurement the run existed to keep honest, and would collapse deferred into unmet in exactly the way specDoc.ts:8-13 forbids by name. The debt the gate reports is real and is tracked: clause-2, clause-3 and clause-5 are live records with spec null, findable by tasks list --deferred, and c3 is named as the acceptance test for c4 of the-workflow-records-what-cost-it-in-one-place. What the gate is actually missing is a state for 'unmet, permanently, and discharged elsewhere', which is filed as spec-done-defer-open-gives-an-unmet-clause-record-the-same-s. A red gate with a recorded reason is more honest than a green one bought by changing a verdict, and this is the second half of the same finding rather than a workaround for it.

head: 16605047e68d245abf44f9d8edbb2c9c21006fd5
note: REFRAME, by the author, 2026-08-06, and it supersedes the premise the orchestrated run was built on. The question a workflow must answer for every decision is WHO DECIDES IT MOST DURABLY, not how to protect the author's time. Human attention being scarce is true and is not the principle; it is a consequence. Mechanical decisions genuinely belong to the worker that has just read the code, because it holds the freshest and most specific knowledge and routing one upward makes the decision both worse and slower. Planning decisions genuinely belong to the planner-and-author pairing, because that pairing has the best model of what is coming and its decisions are therefore least likely to be re-decided or rewritten. Each role has a domain where its decisions hold. THE TEST IS DURABILITY: a decision made in the wrong place gets re-decided, and the re-decision is the cost. That is a better metric than counting how many times a human entered the loop, because it measures whether the placement was right rather than whether the author was disturbed. The run's own log already contains the evidence and it was read the wrong way at the time. Three patterns it recorded as worker or auditor failures are all misplacement: the 18:42:16Z entry where the orchestrator's pass-1 ruling on spec ownership was re-ruled at pass 2 in its own words as 'I named a threshold where the case wanted an invariant'; the 16:00:12Z entry where the orchestrator's correction to c2 named one site that was dead code; and fix-the-neighbour, three for three across three branches. Every one is a decision that did not hold, and every one was made mid-run by the orchestrator rather than by a planner. So run-an-orchestrator c3 is wrong as written, not merely unmet: 'the orchestrator does not adjudicate' is a blanket prohibition where a placement question was wanted, and a blanket prohibition is the same error as enumerating four classes where two axes were wanted. c3 stays unmet in the record because the run did fail it as written, and this decision is why the successor clause is not a stricter version of it.

head: 405eb154b5b8e0c643acd129b0f9e062f38cb88e
note: DURABILITY RATE MEASURED, 2026-08-06, over 24 specs carrying 55 audit passes and 470 clause gradings. Method: a clause grading is a judgement, and two different decisions hide in the sequence of them. A FIX is the decision made between a pass grading cN unmet and the next pass grading cN; it held if the next grading is met. A CERTIFICATION is a pass grading cN met; it held if no later pass reverses it. Gradings of unknown are excluded because nobody looked, and a pass whose head SHA equals the previous pass's is a re-grade of unchanged code rather than a fix. This spec's own pass 2 is excluded from the fix population by name: it re-graded c2/c3/c5 of run-an-orchestrator unmet with no fix attempted, because that run cannot be re-run, and counting it would measure the measurement. RESULT, whole repository: 23 fixes of which 7 did not hold, a 30.4 percent fix failure rate, against 428 certifications of which 2 were reversed, 0.5 percent. RESULT, the four branches of the orchestrated run: 10 fixes of which 6 did not hold, 60 percent, against 84 certifications of which 0 were reversed. THE CROSS-RUN COMPARISON IS CONFOUNDED and must not be reported as it stands: the run's briefs were sharper, and a sharper brief finds more too-small fixes without the fixing having got worse, which is the exact hazard ORCHESTRATOR_LESSONS already names. What survives the confounder is the WITHIN-RUN comparison, because one set of auditors under one set of briefs produced both numbers: the same agents who reversed zero of 84 certifications got 6 of 10 fixes wrong. Detection and repair are different competences and this workflow is near-perfect at the first and poor at the second. That is the placement thesis with a number on it: a certification judges what the reader just read, which is the reader's own domain, while a fix judges what the clause promises, which needs the horizon a finding's text does not carry - and every one of the seven failures is a fix aimed at a finding's literal words. KNOWN UNDERCOUNT, and it runs one way: a ruling re-ruled inside a single pass cycle never produces a second unmet verdict and is invisible to this method. The 18:42:16Z spec-ownership re-ruling is exactly that shape, so the true rate is higher than 30.4 and specifically higher for orchestrator rulings. Hand-classified separately and reported with its own small n: 7 substantive orchestrator rulings in the run, 3 later rewritten.

head: ea6262fada438d58a821ed0d43786fba52deac4f
note: Durability data point, n=1, recorded against the measurement rather than folded into it. The lesson-handle worker hit a fix-the-neighbour instance and closed BOTH halves before any audit saw either. It fixed c6, mutation-tested it, found a real survivor - findLesson could answer an unknown id with a fallback and the whole suite stayed green, because the tests pinned that every live id resolves and never that a dead one does not - and fixing that exposed the neighbour, unknownLessonIds computing 'is this citation live' a second time so a loose-matching version of the same bug was reachable through the other door. It now filters through findLesson, leaving one place that answers the question. Verified independently: the code reads as reported and 31 tests pass. WHAT THIS IS AND IS NOT EVIDENCE FOR. Every one of the run's six failed fixes cost an audit pass to detect; this one cost zero, which is the difference the durability measurement is about. But the mechanism that surfaced it was mutation testing, not the dispatch instruction, and WORKER_LESSONS has carried 'a test that cannot fail is not proof' since briefs-carry-the-lessons landed. So the honest attribution is that mutation testing found it and the worker owning its own fix is what let it close both halves without a round trip - not that telling a worker its mechanical decisions are its own made it more careful. n=1 against a 30 percent baseline measured over 23 fixes is not a rate and must not be reported as one. The thing to watch across the next branches is narrower and testable: whether the SECOND half gets closed in the same sitting, since that is the half the measured failures all missed.

head: 4576e5f3cb9a8d045f64800d563b908307d62db0
note: TRIAL MERGE of both live branches, run before either is audited to completion, and it answers the one thing that could have wrecked this batch. a-record-carries-its-fault adds two fields to Task, which rewrites all 653 store lines - docs/tasks.jsonl shows 1306 changed lines - so the per-record region separation the-task-store-survives-parallel-branches bought is worth nothing against it and the whole file is one conflict hunk. Merged lesson-handle first, then friction-record, on a throwaway branch. TWO conflicts, both expected and both mechanical. docs/tasks.jsonl: one hunk spanning the entire file. Resolution is NOT a textual merge and must not be attempted as one - take HEAD's records, which are the only side holding every record including the sibling's additions, and let the new code re-save them. Verified: the new parser round-trips the old shape, 656 records, 0 errors, fault absent renders null exactly as the worker reported. docs/audits/systems.json: one hunk, both branches appending a concept at the same array position, which is the shared-append-point defect already filed as systems-json-is-the-next-shared-append-point and the same shape the store fix does not cover. Resolution is keep both, by hand. Result after resolving: tsc clean, 1806 of 1806 tests pass. The single failure seen before committing was doctor.test.ts asserting against ambient repository state while MERGE_HEAD existed, which is doctor-test-fails-mid-merge and not this batch's; it passed the moment the merge was committed, which is that finding demonstrated rather than argued. CARRY FORWARD, and it is a planning fact rather than a tooling one: the worker recorded it too, independently, as its ninth decision. A branch that adds a field to Task must be SEQUENCED against every other store-writing branch, never run beside them. Three-wide parallelism held for the shared-file case and does not hold for a schema change, and nothing in tasks plan reports the difference - a writes grant on taskStore.ts looks identical whether the branch adds a field or edits a function.

note: Planning defect in my own decomposition, found by the fixer rather than by me, and corrected here. c6 has two halves - a handle that survives rewording, and a citation naming no live lesson being REPORTED rather than silently dropped - and I assigned the whole clause to a-lesson-has-a-handle-that-survives-rewording-it, whose grant is briefLessons.ts alone. The second is not: unknownLessonIds is correct, mutation-proven and has NO CALLER anywhere outside its own test, because no store field carries a citation and no command reports one. So c6's reporting half is met at the unit and unmet end to end, and the branch that would close it - the query, plus the field a record cites from - is one-query-over-the-channel-and-the-second-place-retired. This is the same error the round has now made three times in different clothes: I stated a clause as one property when it spans two write regions, which is the decomposition equivalent of enumerating instances where an invariant was wanted. The correction is not to split c6, because the two halves are one promise and splitting them would let a branch ship a handle nothing can cite and call the clause done. It is to make the second owner explicit: one-query-over-the-channel-and-the-second-place-retired now discharges c6 alongside c1, c5, c7, c8 and c9, so tasks spec show names both owners and neither branch can close the clause alone. The auditor's met verdict on c6 stands for what the handle slice owed and is not disturbed - a clause with two owners is outstanding until both have landed, which is what the standing already computes.

head: 8030052bcd10b00d5f21f15c9442e1cfe33b683f
note: c4's verdict stands and c4's TEXT is amended, which is the opposite of overruling the auditor and is the honest disposition. The auditor graded c4 met on its enumerated promises - file, address, halt exactly the dependents, release on both closes - and filed a HIGH saying nothing reads Task.decider. I verified that HIGH directly: filed a question addressed to the author, ran work-prompt on it, and got 'You are implementing trial-question-which-role-decides-this' plus an instruction to correct its write grant and register what it produces. The addressee is displayed and routes nothing, so the escalation path loops back to a worker as work to implement. c4's closing sentence says 'the addressee is the point rather than a label on it', and it is a label. But that sentence sits after an enumerated list, and an auditor reading the list as the promise and the sentence as rationale is making a defensible reading of a clause I wrote ambiguously. THE CLAUSE MIXED AN ENUMERATION WITH THE INVARIANT IT WAS SUPPOSED TO ILLUSTRATE, which is precisely the error PLANNER_LESSONS names first and precisely the error that produced both of the orchestrated run's spec defects. I committed it in the clause text while quoting the lesson against it. So the remedy is to fix the contract, not the verdict: overruling would correct this instance and leave the ambiguity to be re-read by the next auditor, and a decision that gets re-decided is the cost the durability measurement is about. SECOND ERROR, and it is the same one twice: c4 and c6 each span two write regions and I assigned each to one slice. c6's reporting half needs a caller that cannot exist in briefLessons.ts; c4's routing half needs workPrompt.ts, which no task owns. Both were found by the agents doing the work rather than by me. head: 24273e734288061461581d964784c0ce1ed587b8
note: The friction channel records RECURRENCE, and the count is derived rather than stored. Author's proposal, 2026-08-06: before filing, an agent checks the issue does not already exist, then increments a counter or updates the description, so the store does not grow one record per instance. The goal is adopted whole - it is the exact signal the motivating measurement lacked, since the mutation-manifest friction recurred nine times and ranked below a one-off because prose does not aggregate. The MECHANISM is changed on one point, and the repository's own documented reasoning is why. A counter is by construction a field concurrent branches edit, and .gitattributes states that case explicitly as the reason the store is not merge=union: two branches editing one record keep both copies under one id, doctor reports it and exits 0, so CI stays green while every read answers from the first copy forever. The correct resolution of two increments is to add them, which git cannot compute and a human resolving by hand gets wrong. docs/events.jsonl IS union, for the stated reason that two branches appending collide for no reason a human can adjudicate and keeping both is always the answer - which is exactly concurrent agents hitting the same friction. So an occurrence is appended and the count is derived, which is also c3's own principle one layer up: a stored count and a derived count are two answers to one question and would disagree the first time someone closed one without the other. Updating the description is refused for a second reason beyond merging: the nine manifest instances each carried different context, which spec, which pass, what it cost that time, and one description overwritten nine times loses the variation that shows the shape. An appended occurrence keeps one canonical record AND nine distinct observations, which satisfies the author's requirement that the store not grow while losing nothing. On the check itself the author ruled PROMPT, NEVER REFUSE, matching what --writes already does. The asymmetry is the reason: a duplicate is visible and cheap to triage, a wrong merge makes a distinct defect vanish and the count lie. So attaching is a deliberate act and filing new stays the cheap default, because the agent is least able to classify at the moment it has just hit the friction. The prompt is BY PATH and never by title - priorArt already reads every record's writes and files in every state, and plan-prompt's own text says why: a path is the same string for everyone, a title is authored prose two agents will not choose alike.

head: 935b1129559074901932bce5b24308a1ff88f27e
note: The mutate flake is ruled a HIGH by the author, and reading the code makes it worse than the finding that raised it. MECHANISM, exact: TestRun carries failed, passed, total, filesFailed and raw - counts, no identities. Baseline carries failed, total, ran - counts. verdictOf is one line, 'run.failed > wasFailing ? KILLED : SURVIVED'. So a mutation is credited with a kill whenever the FAILURE COUNT RISES, and the tool never asks WHICH test failed. A flaky test failing during the mutation run is indistinguishable from the mutation's target test failing, and the baseline subtraction cannot help: it corrects for a tree that was already red, not for a tree that goes red intermittently. THE COMPOUNDING, which is the part that makes this high rather than medium: the known flake is three slow spawn-heavy tests - tasks.test.ts, handoff.test.ts, modportal.test.ts - that each pass alone and tip over under FULL-SUITE contention, filed as npm-test-flakes-on-three-slow-spawn-heavy-tests-under-full-s. And mutate's escalation ladder sends a SURVIVED mutation up to whole-suite scope. So the step designed to catch a survivor is the step most exposed to manufacturing a false kill. The tool is least trustworthy exactly where it is doing its most important job, and a false KILLED is the dangerous direction because it reads as proof: a clause graded met on a mutation nothing actually killed. EXPOSURE: every mutation verdict in this repository, including every one cited in this session. It was caught only because an auditor re-ran an identical entry and got a different verdict, which nothing asks anyone to do. THE FIX IS AN INVARIANT AND MUST BE STATED AS ONE, because a fix aimed at the flake's three test names would be the same too-small fix this round has measured seven times: A KILL IS A NAMED TEST GOING FROM PASS TO FAIL, NOT A COUNT GOING UP. Compare identities against the baseline's identities. Whatever the mechanism - a json reporter, or parsing the names already present in raw, which the flake finding itself quotes - the property is that a verdict names the test that changed, and a run where the only newly-failing tests are ones the mutation does not claim is not a kill. Retiring the flake is a separate and lesser fix: the tool must not be able to convert ANY intermittent failure into proof, and there will always be another one.

head: 89c747dd430e5d20a529b391dc5a6a873a81169b
note: Unclassified records are REPORTED AS THEIR OWN BUCKET and are not backfilled. Author's ruling, 2026-08-06. The population is 76, not 470: of 471 reporting-kind records in the store, 238 are done and 157 declined, and a planner asking what to fix in the tooling does not read closed records. 56 open and 20 unreviewed carry no fault, and that number shrinks on its own as they close while every new record must supply one at the point it is assembled. Backfilling would mean assigning a fault to a record whose author is gone, and a guess lands on nobody - the one value c5 exists to protect, because a nobody that becomes the catch-all is emptied of the meaning the whole fault axis depends on. So an honest 'unclassified, and here is how many' beats 76 invented classifications, and the bucket is a third reported category rather than a fourth fault: fault stays exactly tooling, contract or nobody, and absence is absence. This constrains the query slice: unclassified is reported, is excluded from every rate presented as a defect measure for the same reason fault-nobody is, and is never silently folded into any of the three. Recorded because the alternative reading - that the query may treat a missing fault as nobody - would look like a small convenience and would quietly destroy c5.

head: 536cf25f1f28ef2e5db14445bbe1440c52e20735
note: Per-test identity for a mutation verdict is parsed out of the FAIL lines already in the captured vitest output, not taken from the JSON reporter. mutate already depends on the default reporter for its tally, so a second reporter adds a second parse dependency without removing the first; attribution needs only the failing set, which the default reporter names in full; and the JSON reporter writes a file per run, multi-megabyte at whole-suite scope, into a tool whose design is about leaving the tree byte-identical. The tally count and the parsed names are independent readings of the same run, so a reporter format the parse cannot read is caught by their disagreement rather than producing a wrong verdict silently. Names are read from stderr only, the same containment the tally has on stdout. More names than failures is accepted and fewer is refused: measured on vitest 4.1.9, a suite whose beforeAll throws prints a FAIL line for the suite while its tests count as skipped.

head: 536cf25f1f28ef2e5db14445bbe1440c52e20735
note: c3's boundary for 'attributable to the mutation' is reproduction, not the manifest entry's declared tests and not a reachability rule over imports. The entry's own tests scope was rejected on measurement: it makes the whole-suite rung incapable of ever reporting a kill, which deletes the only reason the escalation ladder exists, and it protects nothing at all for an entry that declares no tests, which is where a hand-written manifest most needs it. A reachability rule is more machinery and is wrong in both directions. So every kill, at any scope, is re-measured once with the mutant still on disk against the files its named tests live in; a failure that does not happen again is UNSTABLE, named, and neither a kill nor a survivor. This is not the retry loop the spec's Decisions rule out: it runs once, it can only downgrade a verdict, and it never resolves an unstable one. The same second measurement is what discharges c4 for a kill found at the scope it is confirmed at. Survivors are not confirmed, because a false SURVIVED costs an argument and a false KILLED reads as proof; what a SURVIVED can still say is free, and the row names any test the baseline saw fail and the mutated run saw pass.

head: 536cf25f1f28ef2e5db14445bbe1440c52e20735

Registering one would put a second name on a file whose job did not change, and audit-status reports two concepts claiming one file as the signal that the file does two jobs - which would be a false report here.

head: cfa38dedce0d6dddc355fe73a25e3b9bdb109c2b
note: doctor KEEPS EXACTLY ONE FAILURE CONDITION. Author's ruling, 2026-08-06, refusing c5 of a-record-cannot-leave-the-store-unrecorded as it was written. CLAUDE.md states the single condition - a line that will not parse - in two places, and separately says a gate earns its place by preventing something that actually happened rather than by sounding rigorous. The spec's argument was that proof-targets-resolve IS that instance, which is coherent and is still not enough: one historical absence is the case for REPORTING it, not for failing the build on the store's own history. So the clause is not deleted, it is INVERTED into a refusal - doctor keeps one condition, and an unexplained absence is named, counted and printed on every run that finds one while changing no exit code. A deleted clause leaves the gate available to the next branch that finds the argument locally reasonable; a refusal clause makes re-adding it a visible contract change. Same instrument as c3 of the friction channel (blocking is derived, never stored) and c9 (nothing gates), both of which exist because the reasonable-sounding alternative had to be refused in writing rather than merely not built. WORTH RECORDING AS A PATTERN, because this is the SECOND time today: the lesson-handle audit found indexLessons throwing at module load and I ruled that doctor must not gain a second failure condition there either, and now a spec written in another context proposed the same shape from a different direction. Two independent proposals in one day, each locally reasonable, both toward the same gate. That is the drift CLAUDE.md's retirement of the 5 percent comment budget was about - a gate that generates work and cannot prove what it claims - and the cheap defence is that each refusal is written into a clause rather than won in conversation and forgotten.

head: b54a24347ef4fe5bb69f72529985296925ed2a65
note: LESSON ELEVATION IS FLAGGED, NEVER TRIGGERED, and there is no threshold anywhere in code. Author's ruling, 2026-08-06, refining an earlier proposal of count>3. The signal is a session tripping over one lesson repeatedly IN A WAY THAT IMPEDED WORK, and the response is a planning task asking whether the lesson should stop being an instruction and become a step. Three things fall out and each removes machinery rather than adding it. FIRST, the impeded-work qualifier is not a new field: it is the channel's own admission criterion. This channel records what working the process cost, so a breach that cost nothing was never a friction record in the first place, and a breach caught by an audit cost that audit pass. Nothing needs to carry a flag saying it mattered. SECOND, the flag is a record in this same channel and not a second system, which means it dedupes by c11 and accumulates by c10 for free: one record per lesson, N occurrences, each saying where it cost. THIRD, wants-a-planner is an existing state - roadmap.ts's own comment says unspecced wants a planning session where ready wants an implementer - so the flag surfaces in a queue that already reads correctly with no new noun. The number is a READING AID FOR A HUMAN AND NEVER A RULE THE TOOL APPLIES. Seeing seven occurrences against one lesson is how a planner knows to consider escalation; no code compares that seven to anything. The reason is measured rather than stylistic: a stated threshold has been the wrong instrument four separate times in this repository within one day, including the orchestrator's own words 'I named a threshold where the case wanted an invariant', and a count is confounded by attention besides - ORCHESTRATOR_LESSONS already records that a sharper brief finds more, so a raw breach count measures how hard anyone looked. That is why c8's denominator has to be per-lesson and why c7's checked-and-clean marker is where it comes from; both clauses already say so as invariants and neither needs amending. WHAT THE EVIDENCE SAYS ABOUT THE FIRST CANDIDATE: the mutation-proof lesson was breached seven times in one 3.5-hour run, recorded live as 'Seventh false-proof test of the run'. It is already an imperative naming its own command, so rewording cannot help it - which is exactly the case the recorded three remedies (badly worded, wrong brief, wrong) do not cover, and the case elevation exists for. The control is next to it: audit-prompt carries mutation as step 4 of a numbered procedure and work-prompt carries it as lesson 2 of a list, and auditors mutate reliably while workers do not. So elevation has a concrete meaning needing no new machinery - a lesson graduates out of the lessons list and into the brief's numbered procedure.

note: gui-rebuild is split in two, and the seam goes first. The author's requirement (2026-08-07) is that the GUI and the REPL cannot drift in capability or function and that the GUI cannot alter state directly. Neither is achievable inside src/ui: the command set lives in scripts/play-cli.ts at layer scripts, which src/ui may not import, and formatInventory/formatState already read GameState, so even the REPL reaches past the published view. A driver written against this tree must grow a second path. So a-driver-renders-the-play-surface-and-cannot-extend-it lands first and makes identity structural -- one command table, derived help, no reachable GameState -- and gui-rebuild owns the behavioural half, one scripted sequence replayed through both drivers landing on byte-identical state, which needs two drivers to exist. Splitting rather than bundling follows result-application-seam's recorded reasoning, and harder: a 909-line restructure inside a diff that also adds a directory would be reviewed as incidental.

head: b56ba3ee30365f83e10738189ac42d94bcad295c
note: The five gui-rebuild members are a serial chain over src/ui, on purpose. tasks plan reports the concentration and it is right: one new directory is one region, and CLAUDE.md's own advice is that chunks touching one file are one change and that more workers on it buy nothing. The chain exists so a worker's context holds one piece -- shell, then real time, then the map and character tabs, then the harness, then the two claims only the finished driver can prove -- not so four of them can run at once. Ordering them by requires is the honest encoding: unordered tasks over one region would be a defect the moment any of them committed its grant.

That conflated an action's owner with its actor - 'fight:' is authored under '# entity giant-rat' but the player is who performs it, which is why the player has no '# entity' and the global '# stat' bases are their sheet (non-entity-action-owner-inherits-player-stats). 'on hit self:' on a fight: lands on the player and always would have; the fixture table stands. Only the second finding is real: a persistent effect's results must be able to name the other party in the moment, which this spec's own thorns fixture already requires since damage-taken identifies the struck actor and thorns must reach the attacker. Granted that, all four fixtures are expressible as persistent effects and archetype-mods authors them that way by preference, not by necessity.

note: New trigger, sighted 2026-08-07: worktree CLEANUP empties the shared node_modules, not only an install. Afterwards node_modules held 0 entries and every tsx/vitest/tsc invocation in the main checkout failed; npm ci restored 228 packages. Any fix should cover both directions, and the safe cleanup order is: remove the junction first, then the directory.

head: be2d5ea3b2629a157d46a02a9c60ddbc23780603
note: The task system is frozen after this push, and freezing does not include a first whole-system sweep. Ruled by the author 2026-08-07. Task system has lastAudit null and has never been swept as its own system, only at branch level; the argument for sweeping before a freeze is that defects in it will bite the MVP work that runs through it. The argument against won: this push clears fifteen HIGHs, which is the signal a sweep exists to produce, and a sweep commissioned at the moment work is stopping produces findings whose only possible disposition is deferral. The freeze is recorded instead as a note and a lastAudit SHA on the Task system entry in systems.json, set by the last branch of the push, so a later reader sees a deliberate stop rather than a system nobody got to.

head: be2d5ea3b2629a157d46a02a9c60ddbc23780603
note: Ownership is declared file by file and coverage keeps its own field. Ruled by the author 2026-08-07, answering 'remove all directory ownership from systems.json so a new file cannot join the wrong system by accident'. A system's paths becomes exact files only and checkManifest refuses a directory there, which is what makes the accident impossible: an undeclared file is owned by nobody and audit-status already exits non-zero on exactly that. The deliberate double coverage directory grants currently create must not die with them, so it moves to its own field: covers, directories, audit window only, conferring no ownership. DSL load path declares covers src/content and keeps its second read of the contribution files; Testing procedure drops its scripts/lib grant rather than restating it, because its own audit already filed that window as accidental. This makes the manifest say what CLAUDE.md already says -- ownership single-valued, coverage many-to-many -- instead of deriving both from one list. unowned keeps its directory and glob grants: a new file under docs attributes nothing to any system, and enumerating a hundred audit records is churn with no accident to prevent.

head: be2d5ea3b2629a157d46a02a9c60ddbc23780603
note: the-workflow-records-what-cost-it-in-one-place closes on its HIGHs, and c13 is abandoned. Ruled by the author 2026-08-07 scoping the final push before the freeze. Its two in-flight branches merge, its three remaining HIGH members land, and a-lesson-can-be-retired-and-the-retirement-is-recorded -- the one medium member, sole owner of c13 -- is declined with the clause abandoned rather than deferred. Retiring a lesson is the only clause whose absence costs nothing while the system is frozen: no lesson will be retired if no branch is editing lessons. head: f9161c14622d91f74c5883ce43658026e87bc13b
note: A branch's active specs are a set, read from the records its own store diff changed, and no heuristic picks one of them. Ruled by the author 2026-08-08. The inference was not merely unreliable, it was lossy by type: SpecFacts.written is string[] (mergeReady.ts:265), survives the touchedWriteRegion filter as a set, and is then collapsed to a scalar by specToGrade (mergeReady.ts:256) into BranchStanding.spec: string | null (mergeReady.ts:57). specToGrade, authoredAsPlan and specAddsClauseId exist only to choose which member of that set to keep, and resolveActiveSpec's store route did the same thing more crudely by refusing whenever more than one spec had open members -- 25 of them on this branch today. A set represents every permutation the scalar cannot: none, one, many, and the plan-plus-implementation branch authoredAsPlan was written to paper over. The declaration lives in the store rather than a new file: tasks spec add and tasks start already write Task.spec, so the set is the specs named by the records docs/tasks.jsonl changed against merge-base -- derived, but from a committed reviewable artifact rather than an append-only log, naturally set-valued, and wrong answers show up in a diff a reviewer already reads. It also loses no evidence: every op in WORK_OPS (start, stop, done) writes the record itself, so a record in the store diff is exactly the signal branchWorkedOnMembers read out of the log. Rejected: a per-branch tracked file, because it must be created, kept current and removed by hand, which is the manual sync CLAUDE.md forbids; and enforcing branch-name-equals-slug, because it caps a branch at one spec and so does not solve the type problem.

note: The three members of a-branch-is-told-which-spec-it-owes all write mergeReady.ts and are dispatched anyway, because they are serial rather than parallel. tasks plan graded this a defect on the rule that a plan concentrated in one place is one task and more workers on it buy nothing, which is correct about parallelism and is not what the split is for: the members run in a requires chain on ONE branch, so no two workers hold the file at once and nothing merges between them. What the split buys is bounded worker context, not concurrency -- member 1 spent 322k tokens and 138 tool calls on five clauses, and an eleven-clause single task would exceed what one agent can hold well. Phase 3 measured the alternative: two branches over one region cost five shared files, three real conflicts, and one defect neither audit could see, because tasks plan reads forecast paths and cannot know what a fix will actually need. So the grant overlap is deliberate and the requires edges are the mechanism that makes it safe. Recorded rather than dismissed, because the check reported honestly and a future reader should find the reason here instead of assuming the defect was missed.

note: specStanding maps every clause id an own member discharges to a verdict, defaulting to unknown when clauseStandings has no entry for it (a stale/renumbered clause id, or the spec doc failing to parse), rather than filtering the composed standings down to ownClauseIds. Filtering would let a clause id that no longer exists in the spec text silently read as nothing-outstanding; mapping-with-fallback keeps it outstanding (unknown) instead, closing a gap the old whole-spec grading never had to consider because it never scoped by discharges at all. Not required by any single proof clause's literal text but a direct consequence of introducing the scoping c11 asks for.

head: c99b176e18e320d0e0a286852eb6461d503eaa6d
note: When the store diff cannot be read at all (no merge base, or docs/tasks.jsonl unreadable there), the spec leg fails rather than passing as 'declares nothing'. c9 only says the gate must 'say so' about an unreadable diff, not explicitly that it must fail -- but reading unreadable as a silent pass would let a broken checkout merge with real, undetected debt, which is exactly the guess c9 forbids applied to the gate's own go/no-go answer.

note: Pass 1's c1 evidence describes 1978988, and the EPERM regression it filed was fixed after the pass. saveStore now waits out a reader holding the destination -- 500ms, inside the lock it already holds, so no write can be reordered by it -- and converts an exhausted wait into a StoreError carrying the same re-run wording every other store refusal has. head: 342bf645c55d520402ffd5246fa4188cc7636171
note: Ruled 2026-08-08: this branch merges with the a-lesson-is-folded-from-its-own-log legs of merge-ready red, and does not fix the derivation. Three reasons. The leg is advisory — .github/workflows/test.yml runs tsc, npm test, layer-check, audit-status, doctor, spec show and plan, and merge-ready is not among them, so what is red is a human reviewer's read and not a check. The fix turns on a design question this record itself frames and does not answer: which field changes count as working a member, when a triage move and a state change are both edits that touch no promise. And answering it here would be unclaused work on a system this branch froze, needing a clause on a spec and a third audit round to certify. What the branch owes instead is that a reader of the red leg can find this ruling: the leg names the spec, the spec's only open member is this record, and tasks show on it prints this decision.

head: 342bf645c55d520402ffd5246fa4188cc7636171
note: The ordering edge this branch put on a-lesson-is-folded-from-its-own-log stays. Section 7.4 of the 2026-08-08 sweep asked for a ruling on the briefLessons.ts collision and the answer is content-then-fold: two entries in existing arrays cost the fold nothing, while authoring two new lessons against a log format that does not exist costs a round trip. Recording that as a requires edge rather than as prose is what makes the tooling enforce it, and dropping the edge to turn a merge-ready leg green would be letting the gate pick the design. The cost of keeping it is filed as ordering-a-member-declares-its-spec.

note: Observation point: a synchronous observer list carried on the Segment, not a return value and not an accumulated list. The open question left this to the slice. A list read after the segment cannot interleave a consumer's own log lines with the results that caused them, and skill-levels-xp-events' level-up line and combat-events' hooks both have to land next to the result that fired them.

head: 849ec2cbb84fecb88fbbc89b07e616d093716711
note: applyResultsNow keeps its four-parameter signature and names PLAYER at its own call to applyResults rather than gaining an actor parameter. It exists to fire an authored on empty:/on full:/dialogue handler, and poolStores already records that a foe's pool takes the clamp but not the handlers, so there is no subject for it to vary over yet. Adding the parameter would be a forecast; the branch that needs it can add it.

head: 849ec2cbb84fecb88fbbc89b07e616d093716711
note: The modal: log line moved out of the switch and became the observer list's first entry. It narrates an applied result rather than applying one - the modal itself is pendingModal - so it is the refactor, not an improvement bundled into it. It also keeps the list from shipping empty: emptying RESULT_OBSERVERS is killed by four unit test files, which is what proves the seam is wired into the segments the game runs rather than only into the ones a test builds.

head: 849ec2cbb84fecb88fbbc89b07e616d093716711
note: ResultApplication.magnitude is signed, in the result's own units, with count folded in, and reports what actually moved rather than what was asked for - a take: of five from an inventory holding two reports -2. Zero where the kind moves no quantity. Wrappers (chance/contest/gate/one-of/roll) report nothing, and neither does a say: on a repetition that does not lead: they selected, they did not apply.

head: e78972ef506243bca5bd2aeb9039a0a19c284584
note: A modal answer is one key=value pair per line and a modal stays open until every option has one, rather than submit-modal taking a whole form atomically. The spec's own spelling is singular, and a value that runs to the end of the line is what lets a dialogue choice - which holds spaces, dots and punctuation - be an answer at all. The partial answers live in the frame, which is serialisable, so the driver holds no half-form of its own and never has to read a line out of band to complete one; that is what makes c10 structural rather than incidental.

head: e78972ef506243bca5bd2aeb9039a0a19c284584
note: view.choices is empty while any modal is open, and a modal's options are published only through view.modals. The alternative - projecting modal options back into choices as a PlayChoice kind - is the two-mechanism shape c5 exists to remove, one layer up. A driver reads choices for the world and modals for what sits atop it.

The player-facing surface is the choice list, and that is where a modal sits atop the world.

note: Closed by correcting the false claim, not by designing a universal neutral. faction: world, player is now described as at peace with world and player rather than with everyone, and the pairwise limit is named on the page: past two factions a shopkeeper safe from all sides must enumerate every faction, which is the enumeration the same document rejects as the reason # entitytype loses. The two obvious fixes - an everyone wildcard, or peace as a relation between factions rather than as shared membership - are recorded as an open question deciding to starting-zone, the first module with more than two factions. Designing either here would have been a mechanism nobody has a use for.

head: 3a0716e6b8fd9f2f993c67c06c98cf784a26bc62
note: Closed by naming it as a place the invariant does not hold, not by giving the log a subject. A handler's say: is written in the player's voice whoever triggered it, so 'You put down another rat.' is wrong the moment Miki does the killing. The document previously claimed log lines have no subject and are unaffected by credit:, which described the limit rather than admitting it; it is now the first of three entries under 'Where it does not hold', and the residual is an open question deciding to whoever gives the log a subject - plausibly combat-events, whose persistent effects have the same problem.

note: skill-levels-xp-events splits at the curve: c7-c9 (the gain grammar and the closed nine-moment set) leave for xp-from-events, ordered behind full-refactor-of-enemies-and-combat. Five of the nine (damage-dealt, damage-taken, missed, evaded, escaped) are defined in terms of a swing and a participant the refactor rewrites, and three (succeeded, failed, escaped) were written against on success:/on failure:/on escape: - blocks the refactor renames, repoints or deletes for combat actions. Authoring nine names in one grammar and rewriting them in the next is what docs/combat/encounter-grammar.md refused twice already, for combat-events and starting-zone. The curve half names no combat concept and no actor, is unblocked today, and is what cooking-vs-dish-complexity and skill gating actually wait on, so it keeps the slug and the record.

head: 14b43cd9f3c1ffe72724cd4415c276100cada0b8
note: The engine's xp moments fold into # event's trigger: field rather than becoming a second on-vocabulary. Ruled by the author 2026-08-09. The alternative - a handler writing on <authored-event>: while a grant writes a trailing on <engine-moment> - is distinguishable by a parser and not by a reader, and 'a reader holding only the page can say what a field refers to' is the invariant the encounter grammar exists to hold. Folding puts the closed set where trigger: on empty already is, and turns arity into the presence of resource: rather than a positional argument. succeeded/failed/escaped collapse to completed/unfinished, which is the real pair once attempts: replaces escape after N.

note: c11 walk, items-mods-and-crafting: c11, c15 and c21 are all expressible against the built substrate and none needs a substrate change. c11 is createInstance('item', itemId, {plane, allocations, experience}) with inventory[itemId] decremented - the payload is opaque so the plane never reaches this module. c15's cluster effect is a record inside that same payload, so jewels stay stackable and uninstanced exactly as it says. c21's first half is c6 here; its second half - a slotted jewel or allocated node whose declaration is gone dropped with its point returned - is InstanceKind.repair, which receives the registry and returns one reason per repair, and the point return is arithmetic inside the item payload that this module never sees.

head: 9960ace81729d318885ea60044104237801a43bf
note: c11 walk, the combat spawn model: expressible with no substrate change. An entity declaring skills: is createInstance('entity', entityId, <per-skill experience>) with templateLoaded asking registry.entities, and the payload naming skill ids is repaired through the same hook when a skill leaves the registry. allies: spawns and a location's respawn deficit are not instances under the settled grammar and never reach this table. Instance ids stay unwritten and unparsed, which is why the id is a runtime counter and no grammar round-trips it.

head: 9960ace81729d318885ea60044104237801a43bf
note: c11 walk, the two things it did surface, one fixed here and one left to the consumer. Fixed: pruneInstances was placed after the record prunes, so an inventory or equipped entry holding an instance id would have asked a table not yet settled - the exact failure c5 says must not happen. It now runs first in pruneStateForRegistry, pinned by a test on warning order and mutation-verified by moving it back. Left: SAVE_FIELDS' RecordPrune.loaded takes (registry, id) and no state, so the inventory rule cannot yet ask instanceIsLive. That is items-mods-and-crafting's to widen when it teaches inventory to hold an instance id; widening it here would be a seam with no consumer. One constraint the substrate does not check and both payloads must respect: a payload round-trips through JSON.stringify in serializeSave, so it holds JSON and not a Map or a Set.

head: 08f01e5bf7dbb9b776aa4b54f1ad343d36aaa4e4
note: in-process-module-api pass 3, the zero-generation half for the fourth consecutive spec-pass: all eight clauses are prose with no proof: target, so the brief printed 'none - no proof target on this spec resolved to a test this brief could name' and step 4 handed me nothing. Built an 11-entry manifest by hand after reading session.ts, save.ts, encounter.ts and modals.ts cold; all 11 killed, about 30 minutes. The sharper cost is the one instanced-objects pass 3 named and this pass now confirms on a second spec: pass 2 ran an 11-entry manifest and named its verdicts in the spec's prose, but a name in an audit-pass paragraph is not a runnable artefact, so I could re-run none of them and reinvented six of the eleven from scratch - the four c4 kinds plus the control. Re-running pass 2's exact manifest is the whole question a re-audit asks (did the four survivors become kills), and answering it cost the same 30 minutes it cost pass 2.

head: 08f01e5bf7dbb9b776aa4b54f1ad343d36aaa4e4
note: Fourth occurrence in four passes by four auditors, this time on in-process-module-api pass 3 while measuring view() cost against content/tutorial-island.dsl on two trees. load('node:fs') resolved to <worktree>/node:fs and threw ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND naming that path; rewriting it as await import('node:fs') worked. One round trip, paid twice over because it ran on both trees. Nothing new to read from it: the rule is still not learnable from the message.

head: 08f01e5bf7dbb9b776aa4b54f1ad343d36aaa4e4
note: in-process-module-api pass 3, and a new shape of the same gap. This worktree was handed over already installed, so the brief's six npm commands ran; the cost landed on the merge-base comparison c8 requires instead. Step 0 says everything written outside the repository goes in the temp directory, so I created the base worktree there - and a worktree outside the repository tree has no module resolution at all, because the branch worktrees under .claude/worktrees have no node_modules of their own and resolve upward to the repo root's. A junction to the branch worktree's node_modules therefore creates an empty directory and every npm run in it still fails on tsx. The junction has to point at <repo root>/node_modules. Cost four tool calls and two wrong junctions to work out, and the brief states no environment precondition for the tree it tells you to compare against.

head: 08f01e5bf7dbb9b776aa4b54f1ad343d36aaa4e4
note: Paid twice in one pass on in-process-module-api pass 3, and in both directions. c4 asserts two things: that six named kinds of data are published (now true, and all six killed by named tests) and that a driver cannot reach GameState (false, reproduced through npm run inspect). c8 asserts that nothing observable changed: three earlier measurements of it hold and a fourth, a scripted REPL session over an authored # save, dies on this head where the merge base plays it. Both went down as unmet, which reads as though the publication work and the transcript work had not been done - and both cost a paragraph of evidence explaining which part holds, which is the same tax the first-class-modals c3 occurrence measured. The composed standing line now reads 'outstanding: c1..c8 (unmet)' for a branch that proved four previously unwatched data kinds and sealed a handle two passes could open.

head: 08f01e5bf7dbb9b776aa4b54f1ad343d36aaa4e4
note: Reproduced end to end by pass 3, which is the confirmation the record was filed to get. The implementer removed clause-1,2,3,5,6,7 with a reason and kept clause-4; my pass then graded every clause as the brief instructs and tasks audit recreated all six, plus clause-8. The store now holds eight undelivered members of this spec, six of which duplicate the-command-set-lives-below-the-ui-layer and layer-check-reads-every-source-file - both open, unmerged members of this same spec that already owe exactly those clauses. So the removal did not settle anything: the next auditor who follows its own brief regenerates them, and the branch's spec leg goes red again on debt no member of it owns. Cost me nothing to produce and the branch a second round of the same cleanup.
